messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 57
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Interior Designer
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 72

She is 57, a South Eastern Asian woman who has been married for more than three decades, and she still measures time by the morning everything split into before and after. Before, she is an interior designer with a careful eye and a steady routine. She spends her days moving through clients’ homes and office spaces, noticing proportions, fabrics, light, the way a room can hold or repel a person. She likes order, likes choosing where a chair should sit so that conversation can flow, where a lamp should go so that shadows soften instead of sharpen. Her husband teases that she can walk into any space and immediately feel what is wrong with it. Before, this sensitivity is part of her talent.

The attack happens on an ordinary weekday. She is in a large hotel lobby meeting a client about redesigning a restaurant space. She remembers studying the marble floor, the arrangement of low chairs, the oversized floral display by the entrance. Then there is a blast so loud it seems to come from inside her own body. The air changes first—pressure, heat, dust—then screaming. Glass breaks in a shower. She is thrown sideways, striking her shoulder against a column. For a few seconds she cannot understand what she is seeing: a man on the floor not moving, a woman with blood on her face calling for someone, a child’s shoe with no child in it. She smells smoke and something metallic. Her ears ring so sharply that everyone appears to be moving inside a silent film. She crawls behind an overturned table and presses herself flat against the floor, convinced another explosion is coming. She thinks of her husband, absurdly of the sample boards still in her bag, and then of nothing but getting out alive.

In the weeks afterward, people tell her she is lucky. She has cuts, bruising, and a shoulder injury, but she survives. She says thank you because that is what one says. Inside, she feels no luck at all. She does not sleep for more than an hour or two at a time. When she closes her eyes, the lobby returns with sensory precision: shattered glass in her hair, the smell of burning upholstery, the sight of bodies half-hidden by dust. She wakes with her heart pounding, her nightclothes damp, sometimes already out of bed before she is fully conscious. Her husband reaches for her and she jerks away before she recognizes him. She begins checking the doors repeatedly, then the windows, then the doors again.

At work, the change is obvious to her long before she admits it to anyone else. Hotel projects become impossible. Large public spaces with multiple exits should feel safer, but to her they feel uncontained, vulnerable. She stands in lobbies and restaurants scanning faces, noting unattended bags, calculating distance to stairwells. Instead of noticing color temperature and texture, she tracks threats. Sudden sounds—a dropped tray, a slammed door, construction drilling from another floor—send a shock through her body so intense she grips the nearest surface to steady herself. Once, during a client presentation, a balloon from a nearby event pops, and she drops to a crouch before she can stop herself. The room goes silent. She laughs too quickly and says, “Just nerves,” but afterward she sits in her car shaking, humiliated, unable to drive for nearly an hour.

She starts avoiding more and more. At first it is only hotels, then crowded restaurants, then shopping centers, then any building where security feels unclear. She asks clients to meet by video, says she is streamlining her business, says traffic is too stressful, says she is focusing on residential work. These explanations are partly true, but they conceal how small her life has become. Her husband invites her to weddings, family gatherings, temple events. She finds reasons not to go. If she does go, she positions herself near an exit and never removes her coat. She watches people’s hands. She notices every raised voice. Celebration feels dangerous.

Her husband is gentle, but he does not fully understand why she is no longer the woman who used to love travel, who once delighted in busy markets and ornate old buildings. She sees his confusion when she insists on sitting only in certain corners of a room, when she asks him to text the moment he arrives anywhere, when she becomes irritable over small disruptions. She hears herself snapping at him for leaving a backpack by the front door and immediately feels ashamed. Shame has become familiar: shame that she survived when others did not, shame that she cannot “move on,” shame that her fear now governs both of them.

She says she used to believe spaces could be made welcoming with enough thoughtfulness. Now she enters a room and imagines how easily it could become a trap. Even at home, she startles at the hum of the elevator in their building, at motorcycles backfiring on the street below, at the smell of smoke from a neighbor’s cooking. Her body reacts before her mind can reason with it. On the worst days she feels as if the blast is still happening somewhere just beyond the next wall.

What troubles her most is not only the fear but the theft of her own way of seeing. She built a life from sensitivity to environment, from noticing details that others miss. Now those same instincts have turned against her. She still chooses fabrics, sketches layouts, advises clients on light and flow, but she does it while carrying the lobby inside her, as if one destroyed space has spread into every room she enters.
